claims.claim: AI ethics is the branch of applied ethics that examines moral questions raised by the design, deployment, and use of artificial intelligence systems, which can usefully be treated as decision systems.
Automated algorithms are widely used to make or support consequential decisions about people, including in education, access to credit, healthcare, and employment.

AI systems can reproduce or amplify bias: NIST reports that biases are endemic across technology processes and can lead to harmful impacts regardless of intent, and that AI can newly introduce or amplify biases.
Bias can enter at different points: through the training data, through design and algorithm choices, and through feedback effects in which a system's outputs shape the data it later receives.

Documented machine-bias cases reported in the research literature include gender bias in hiring tools, racial disparities in credit and parole risk assessments, and facial recognition systems performing worse on darker skin tones.

Many AI systems are opaque ('black box'): the people affected by a decision often cannot know how the output was produced, and with some machine-learning systems even the developers do not fully know which patterns in the data drove the result.

The ACM identifies three sources of opacity in algorithmic decisions: technical (the algorithm does not lend itself to easy explanation), economic (transparency can be costly or compromise trade secrets), and social (revealing inputs can violate privacy expectations).

There is a live debate over whether opaque AI decisions are acceptable: some ethicists argue for explainability or a right to justification, while others argue that what matters is whether machine decisions are well calibrated, and explainable AI (XAI) is an active technical field.

Responsibility for AI-related harms is hard to allocate because many actors are involved (data collectors, developers, deployers, users, regulators); philosophers have discussed a 'responsibility gap' in which neither the machine nor any individual human is clearly responsible, and proposals such as keeping humans 'in the loop' or in 'meaningful control' are debated.
AI systems depend on large amounts of personal data, and privacy debates cover surveillance by states, companies, and individuals, with regulation described as slow to respond.
Technical AI safety, sometimes called alignment, is an active research area closely related to AI ethics but not identical to it; its definitions and goals are contested.

Responses to automation's labor effects range from alarmed to neutral to optimistic; historical productivity gains have not necessarily meant net job loss, though job polarization (growth at high- and low-skill ends with pressure on mid-skill jobs) is a documented pattern.

Since roughly 2015-2020 many organizations, including governments, the EU, companies, and professional associations, published AI ethics principles; a comparative review of 84 sets of guidelines found strong convergence on principles such as transparency, justice and fairness, non-maleficence, responsibility, and privacy.

Most AI ethics principles are voluntary and non-binding; critics describe some as 'ethics washing' or toothless, defenders treat them as useful work in progress, and implementation, enforcement, and power are the central limits of principle-based approaches.
Some jurisdictions have moved toward binding regulation, notably the EU's AI Act, which regulates AI applications by risk level.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Are opaque AI decisions acceptable when they are effective?
positions: Some ethicists argue decisions affecting people's lives must be explainable or justifiable to them, treating explainability as a basic ethical criterion.

Others argue that a right to explanation may not be what is actually needed, and that what matters is whether machine decisions are well calibrated; explainable AI research itself disagrees about whether interpretability means causal explanation, justification, or trust.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented as an open trade-off debate in the lesson; neither position is endorsed.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Can bias in AI be fixed by technical means?
positions: Some argue fairness can be engineered through better datasets and fairness-aware algorithms.

Others argue technical fixes have inherent limits because a mathematical definition of fairness is hard to agree on, and different fairness definitions can conflict; NIST emphasizes that zero risk of bias is not achievable and that systemic, statistical, and human factors all matter.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports both the technical mitigation efforts and the limits, attributing the skeptical position to the cited literature.

conflictingEvidence.issue: What will automation mean for employment?
positions: Alarmed: large shares of jobs are susceptible to computerization.
Neutral/optimistic: past productivity gains did not necessarily reduce overall employment, and AI may generate more employment; job polarization is a documented intermediate pattern.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented neutrally as a contested empirical and normative question.

positions: Critics: principles are meaningless, toothless, politically harmful, and can function as 'ethics washing'.
Defenders: principles are useful work in progress toward operationalization and enforcement.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both positions attributed and described factually; the lesson notes most principles are voluntary.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Does AI create a genuine 'responsibility gap'?
positions: Some philosophers argue that with autonomous systems neither the human nor the machine may be responsible for harms.
Others argue the difficulty is temporary confusion in allocating responsibility among humans, not a genuine gap; keeping humans in the loop or in meaningful control is proposed but debated.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented as an open philosophical question.

sourceRecords.title: Towards a Standard for Identifying and Managing Bias in Artificial Intelligence (NIST Special Publication 1270)
sourceRecords.provider: National Institute of Standards and Technology, U.S. Department of Commerce
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (U.S. federal government). Read the PDF (March 2022, 86 pages) on 2026-08-21. Supports claims that biases are endemic across technology processes, harmful impacts can occur regardless of intent, AI can newly introduce or amplify biases, bias has systemic, statistical, and human categories, and zero-risk of bias is not achievable; mitigation challenges span datasets, testing/evaluation, and human factors. Reference-only; prose synthesized.

sourceRecords.title: Statement on Algorithmic Transparency and Accountability
sourceRecords.provider: ACM U.S. Public Policy Council and ACM Europe Policy Committee
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (professional body). Read the PDF (approved by USACM January 2017 and ACM Europe May 2017) on 2026-08-21. Supports claims about the ubiquity of algorithmic decisions in education, credit, healthcare, and employment; the technical/economic/social sources of opacity; bias entering through input data or algorithms; and the call to hold institutions using analytics to the same standards as human decision-makers. Reference-only; prose synthesized.
